REPRODUCTIVE__Testis (seminiferous tubul:
Overview — The Male Gonad’s Two Jobs

The testis does two things at once: it makes sperm (an exocrine, spermatogenic role) inside the seminiferous tubules, and it makes testosterone (an endocrine role) from the Leydig cells in the surrounding interstitium.

🔬 Image slot — testis at low power — packed seminiferous tubules with germinal epithelium, separated by interstitium containing Leydig cells
  • A dense capsule, the tunica albuginea, sends septa in to divide the testis into lobules.
  • Each lobule holds 1–4 coiled seminiferous tubules that drain into the rete testis → epididymis.
Two compartments, two cell families: the tubule (Sertoli + germ cells → sperm) and the interstitium (Leydig cells → testosterone).
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — seminiferous tubule cross-sections — stratified germinal epithelium, tall Sertoli cells, and clusters of eosinophilic Leydig cells between tubules
  • Seminiferous tubules cut in cross-section, lined by a thick, stratified germinal (spermatogenic) epithelium.
  • A lumen containing tails of spermatozoa in active tubules.
  • Leydig cells — clusters of eosinophilic cells in the interstitium between tubules.
  • Sertoli cells — tall columnar cells spanning the epithelium, with a pale nucleus and a prominent nucleolus.
Seminiferous tubules + interstitial Leydig cells → testis. The stratified germ-cell layers maturing toward a sperm-filled lumen are unmistakable.
The Seminiferous Tubule & Spermatogenesis
🔬 Image slot — spermatogenic sequence — spermatogonia at the base maturing through spermatocytes and spermatids to luminal spermatozoa

Germ cells mature from the basement membrane toward the lumen:

1
Spermatogoniadiploid stem cells at the base
2
Primary spermatocyteslargest cells; undergo meiosis I
3
Secondary spermatocytes → spermatidsmeiosis II; haploid, short-lived
4
Spermatozoaspermiogenesis → released into lumen
Primary spermatocytes are the largest, most conspicuous germ cells (their condensed meiotic chromatin stands out). Spermiogenesis is the final remodelling of round spermatids into streamlined spermatozoa.
Sertoli Cells & the Blood–Testis Barrier
  • Tall columnar cells extending from basement membrane to lumen; they support and nourish the germ cells.
  • Tight junctions between adjacent Sertoli cells form the blood–testis barrier, splitting the epithelium into a basal (spermatogonia) and an adluminal (meiotic cells) compartment.
  • They phagocytose residual bodies and secrete androgen-binding protein (ABP), inhibin, and (in the fetus) anti-Müllerian hormone.
  • FSH acts on Sertoli cells; inhibin feeds back to suppress FSH.
The blood–testis barrier keeps developing (haploid) sperm immunologically hidden. If it is breached (trauma, vasectomy, infection) the immune system can form anti-sperm antibodies.
Leydig Cells & Hormonal Control
🔬 Image slot — interstitium — clusters of eosinophilic Leydig cells with lipid droplets and Reinke crystals between the tubules
Leydig cells
  • Interstitial, eosinophilic, lipid-rich; contain Reinke crystals
  • Secrete testosterone under LH control
Sertoli cells
  • Respond to FSH
  • Make ABP (keeps intratubular testosterone high) & inhibin
LH → Leydig → testosterone; FSH → Sertoli. High local testosterone (bound to ABP) plus FSH together drive spermatogenesis; inhibin and testosterone provide negative feedback.
The Duct System — From Tubule to Vas
🔬 Image slot — excurrent ducts — rete testis, ciliated efferent ductules, and the epididymis with stereocilia
1
Straight tubules → rete testisSertoli-only tubuli recti into a network in the mediastinum
2
Efferent ductulesciliated; reabsorb testicular fluid (scalloped lining)
3
Epididymispseudostratified columnar with stereocilia; sperm mature & are stored
4
Vas deferensthick three-layer smooth muscle
Epididymis = pseudostratified columnar epithelium with long stereocilia and a smooth luminal border of stored sperm — a classic slide.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Cryptorchidism
Undescended testis → impaired spermatogenesis and increased germ-cell tumour risk
Testicular torsion
Twisted spermatic cord → ischaemia; a surgical emergency (sudden pain, high-riding testis)
Seminoma
Commonest germ-cell tumour; sheets of clear “fried-egg” cells with a lymphocytic stroma; may raise LDH/hCG
Non-seminomatous GCTs
Yolk-sac (↑AFP), choriocarcinoma (↑hCG), embryonal carcinoma, teratoma
Klinefelter (47,XXY)
Small firm testes with hyalinised tubules & Leydig hyperplasia → infertility
Varicocele
Dilated pampiniform plexus (“bag of worms”), usually left; a cause of infertility
Mumps orchitis and Sertoli-cell-only syndrome (germ-cell aplasia → tubules lined by Sertoli cells only) are classic causes of azoospermia/infertility.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Seminiferous tubules + interstitial Leydig cells = testis.
Germ cells mature base → lumen: spermatogonia → primary spermatocyte (largest) → spermatid → spermatozoon.
Sertoli cells: support + blood–testis barrier (tight junctions); FSH target; secrete ABP, inhibin, AMH.
Leydig cells: interstitial, eosinophilic, Reinke crystals; secrete testosterone under LH.
LH → Leydig → testosterone; FSH → Sertoli; inhibin feeds back on FSH.
Epididymis = pseudostratified columnar with stereocilia; sperm mature & are stored there.
Seminoma = commonest, fried-egg cells + lymphocytic stroma; yolk-sac → AFP, choriocarcinoma → hCG.
Cryptorchidism raises germ-cell tumour risk; Klinefelter = hyalinised tubules & infertility.
REPRODUCTIVE__Ovary (follicles, corpus l:
Overview — The Female Gonad

The ovary has two roles: producing oocytes (oogenesis) and making the sex hormones oestrogen and progesterone. Its structure is a follicle-packed cortex around a vascular medulla.

🔬 Image slot — ovary at low power — cortex containing follicles at different stages around a central vascular medulla, with a surface epithelium
  • The surface is covered by a simple cuboidal “germinal” epithelium (a misnomer) over the tunica albuginea.
  • The cortex holds the follicles; the medulla carries vessels, lymphatics and nerves.
Everything examinable happens in the cortex: follicles maturing, ovulating, and regressing into a corpus luteum and then a corpus albicans.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — ovarian cortex — primordial, primary and antral follicles, a corpus luteum and a corpus albicans, under a cuboidal surface epithelium
  • Follicles at multiple stages crowded in the cortex — the diagnostic feature.
  • A simple cuboidal surface epithelium over the tunica albuginea.
  • A large, folded corpus luteum and/or a white fibrous corpus albicans scar.
A cortex full of follicles at different stages → ovary. Grade the follicle by its granulosa layer and whether an antrum has formed.
Folliculogenesis — Grading the Follicle
🔬 Image slot — follicle stages — primordial, primary (zona pellucida), secondary antral (theca), and Graafian follicle with cumulus oophorus
Primordial follicle
Primary oocyte + a single layer of flat (squamous) follicular cells; the resting pool
Primary follicle
Single (then multiple) layer of cuboidal granulosa cells; zona pellucida appears; theca begins to form
Secondary (antral) follicle
A fluid-filled antrum appears; theca interna & externa defined; Call–Exner bodies in granulosa
Graafian (mature) follicle
Large antrum; oocyte on a cumulus oophorus with its corona radiata, poised to ovulate
Read two things: the granulosa layer (flat = primordial; cuboidal = primary) and the antrum (present = secondary/Graafian). The zona pellucida is a glycoprotein shell around the oocyte for sperm binding.
The Two-Cell, Two-Gonadotropin Model
Theca interna — LH
  • LH drives production of androgens (androstenedione)
  • Androgens diffuse into the granulosa
Granulosa — FSH
  • FSH induces aromatase → converts androgens to oestrogen
  • Also secretes inhibin (feeds back on FSH)
Theca makes the androgen (LH); granulosa aromatises it to oestrogen (FSH). This division of labour is the two-cell, two-gonadotropin model — and explains why aromatase inhibitors and gonadotropins work where they do.
Ovulation, Corpus Luteum & Corpus Albicans
🔬 Image slot — corpus luteum — folded wall of large pale granulosa lutein cells and smaller peripheral theca lutein cells; adjacent white corpus albicans
1
LH surge → ovulationreleases the secondary oocyte (arrested in metaphase II)
2
Corpus luteumgranulosa + theca lutein cells → progesterone
3
Corpus albicanswhite fibrous scar if no pregnancy (~14 days)
  • The corpus luteum secretes progesterone (and oestrogen) to maintain the endometrium.
  • No pregnancy → it regresses to a corpus albicans; pregnancy → hCG rescues it as the corpus luteum of pregnancy.
  • Most follicles never ovulate — they undergo atresia at any stage.
Corpus luteum = progesterone factory; corpus albicans = its white scar. hCG from a pregnancy keeps the corpus luteum alive until the placenta takes over.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Polycystic ovary syndrome
Multiple subcapsular follicular cysts, thickened tunica, arrested follicles; anovulation + hyperandrogenism
Serous cystadeno(carcinoma)
Commonest ovarian epithelial tumour; psammoma bodies; raised CA-125
Mature teratoma (dermoid)
Germ-cell tumour with tissues from all three layers (hair, skin, teeth); usually benign
Granulosa cell tumour
Sex-cord tumour; Call–Exner bodies; secretes oestrogen & inhibin → precocious puberty / endometrial hyperplasia
Sertoli–Leydig / fibroma
Sertoli–Leydig → androgens (virilisation); fibroma → Meigs syndrome (ascites + pleural effusion)
Endometrioma
Endometriosis in the ovary forming a “chocolate cyst” of old blood
Tumour markers: serous epithelial → CA-125; yolk-sac → AFP; granulosa cell → inhibin; dysgerminoma (the female seminoma) → LDH/hCG.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Cortex full of follicles at various stages + cuboidal surface epithelium = ovary.
Primordial (flat granulosa) → primary (cuboidal + zona pellucida) → secondary/antral (antrum + theca) → Graafian (cumulus oophorus).
Two-cell model: theca (LH → androgen) + granulosa (FSH → aromatase → oestrogen).
Zona pellucida = glycoprotein sperm-binding shell; corona radiata = granulosa around the ovulated oocyte.
LH surge → ovulation; corpus luteum → progesterone; corpus albicans = white scar.
hCG rescues the corpus luteum in pregnancy; most follicles undergo atresia.
Granulosa cell tumour: Call–Exner bodies + oestrogen/inhibin; Sertoli–Leydig → androgens; fibroma → Meigs.
Serous cystadenocarcinoma = commonest, psammoma bodies, CA-125; PCOS = peripheral cysts + hyperandrogenism.
REPRODUCTIVE__Uterus (endometrium — mens:
Overview — A Three-Layered Muscular Organ

The uterus houses and nourishes the embryo. Its wall has three layers, but the examinable action is all in the endometrium, which is remodelled every month by ovarian hormones.

🔬 Image slot — uterine wall — endometrium with glands in stroma, thick myometrium of smooth muscle, and outer perimetrium
1
Endometriummucosa — glands + stroma; cycles monthly
2
Myometriumthick interlacing smooth muscle
3
Perimetriumouter serosa / adventitia
The endometrium has two layers: a stratum functionalis that is shed and rebuilt each cycle, and a stratum basalis that stays put and regenerates it.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — endometrium — simple columnar surface epithelium, tubular endometrial glands set in a cellular stroma, over thick myometrium
  • Endometrial glands (simple columnar) embedded in a cellular stroma — the diagnostic mucosa.
  • A thick myometrium of interlacing smooth-muscle bundles beneath it.
  • The gland shape and stroma tell you the cycle phase (straight vs coiled glands).
Endometrial glands in a cellular stroma over a thick myometrium → uterus. Then date it: straight tubular glands = proliferative; coiled “sawtooth” glands with secretions = secretory.
The Two Endometrial Layers
Stratum functionalis
  • Superficial; shed at menstruation and rebuilt each cycle
  • Supplied by spiral arteries (hormone-sensitive)
Stratum basalis
  • Deep; retained — regenerates the functionalis
  • Supplied by straight (basal) arteries
Spiral arteries feed the functionalis and are the key to menstruation: when hormones fall they constrict, causing the ischaemia that sheds the layer. The basalis and its straight arteries survive to rebuild.
The Menstrual Cycle Phases
🔬 Image slot — cycle phases — menstrual shedding, proliferative straight glands, and secretory coiled glands with glycogen vacuoles and stromal oedema
Menstrual (days 1–4)
Shedding of the functionalis — fragmented glands, blood and stromal breakdown
Proliferative (days 5–14)
Oestrogen-driven regeneration: straight, narrow tubular glands, abundant mitoses, compact stroma
Secretory (days 15–28)
Progesterone-driven: coiled “sawtooth” glands, glycogen vacuoles, luminal secretions, stromal oedema & spiral-artery growth
Oestrogen builds (proliferative); progesterone matures/secretes (secretory). Ovulation at ~day 14 is the switch; the corpus luteum then supplies the progesterone.
Dating the Endometrium & Why Menstruation Happens
  • Straight tubular glands + mitoses → proliferative (oestrogen).
  • Sub-nuclear glycogen vacuoles (~day 16–17) are the first sign ovulation has occurred.
  • Supra-nuclear secretion → luminal secretions → stromal oedema through the mid-secretory phase.
  • Predecidual change & coiled spiral arteries late (~day 23+).
No fertilisation → the corpus luteum regresses → progesterone & oestrogen fall → spiral arteries constrict → ischaemic shedding of the functionalis = menstruation.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Endometrial hyperplasia
Unopposed oestrogen → increased gland:stroma ratio; atypical hyperplasia is premalignant
Endometrial adenocarcinoma
Commonest gynae cancer; postmenopausal bleeding; risk = unopposed oestrogen, obesity, PCOS, tamoxifen, Lynch
Leiomyoma (fibroid)
Commonest uterine tumour; benign whorled smooth muscle; oestrogen-dependent; menorrhagia
Adenomyosis
Endometrial glands & stroma within the myometrium → bulky, tender uterus
Endometriosis
Endometrial tissue outside the uterus → cyclical pain, adhesions, chocolate cysts
Asherman’s syndrome
Damage to the basalis (over-curettage) → intrauterine adhesions, amenorrhoea, infertility
Leiomyosarcoma is the rare malignant smooth-muscle tumour (high mitoses, necrosis, atypia) — distinct from the common benign leiomyoma.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Endometrial glands in a cellular stroma over a thick myometrium = uterus.
Functionalis (shed; spiral arteries) vs basalis (regenerates; straight arteries).
Proliferative = straight tubular glands + mitoses (oestrogen).
Secretory = coiled “sawtooth” glands + glycogen vacuoles + stromal oedema (progesterone).
Sub-nuclear vacuoles (~day 16–17) are the first histological sign of ovulation.
Menstruation = corpus luteum regresses → hormone withdrawal → spiral-artery constriction & ischaemia.
Unopposed oestrogen → hyperplasia → endometrial carcinoma (postmenopausal bleeding).
Fibroid = leiomyoma (whorled, oestrogen-dependent); adenomyosis = endometrium within the myometrium.
REPRODUCTIVE__Fallopian Tube:
Overview — The Oocyte’s Highway

The fallopian (uterine) tube catches the ovulated oocyte, is the site of fertilisation (in the ampulla), and conveys the embryo to the uterus. Its wall is a simple three layers: a highly folded mucosa, a smooth-muscle muscularis, and a serosa.

🔬 Image slot — fallopian tube cross-section — a labyrinth of branching mucosal folds filling the lumen, surrounded by smooth muscle and serosa

It has four regions from ovary to uterus — infundibulum, ampulla, isthmus and intramural part — and no glands or submucosa.

Two cell types line it — ciliated cells that sweep the oocyte toward the uterus and secretory (peg) cells that nourish it — and their balance shifts with the ovarian hormones.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — ampullary mucosa — elaborate branching folds lined by simple columnar epithelium of ciliated and peg cells, with no glands
  • Elaborate, branching (labyrinthine) mucosal folds nearly filling the lumen — most complex in the ampulla.
  • Simple columnar epithelium with two cell types: ciliated and secretory (peg) cells.
  • No glands and no submucosa — separating it from the endometrium.
Labyrinthine mucosal folds + ciliated & peg cells, but NO glands → fallopian tube (the folds are richest in the ampulla).
The Two Epithelial Cells
Ciliated cells
  • Cilia beat toward the uterus to waft the oocyte along
  • Most numerous in the infundibulum/ampulla; oestrogen increases ciliation
Secretory (peg) cells
  • Non-ciliated; secrete nutritive fluid for the oocyte, sperm and embryo
  • Aid sperm capacitation; bulge (“peg”) into the lumen
Oestrogen favours ciliation (and taller cells); progesterone favours secretion (and deciliation). So the epithelium is most ciliated around ovulation, ready to transport the oocyte.
The Four Regions
🔬 Image slot — the four regions — fimbriated infundibulum, wide folded ampulla, narrow muscular isthmus, and intramural segment through the uterine wall
1
Infundibulumfunnel with fimbriae that catch the oocyte
2
Ampullalongest & widest; fertilisation site; most folded
3
Isthmusnarrow, thick muscle, fewer folds
4
Intramuralpasses through the uterine wall into the cavity
  • Muscularis: an inner circular + outer longitudinal smooth-muscle layer whose peristalsis (with the cilia) moves the oocyte.
  • Mucosal folds are most elaborate in the ampulla and progressively simpler toward the isthmus.
The fimbriae sweep over the ovary at ovulation to capture the oocyte; the ampulla is where sperm meet it — both are prime exam facts.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Ectopic pregnancy
Commonest in the ampulla; risk from scarring (PID/surgery); rupture → life-threatening haemorrhage
Salpingitis / PID
Chlamydia/gonorrhoea → inflammation & scarring → infertility, ectopic risk
Hydrosalpinx
A blocked tube distended with clear fluid after chronic inflammation
STIC
Serous tubal intra-epithelial carcinoma at the fimbrial end — precursor of high-grade serous “ovarian” carcinoma (p53)
Primary ciliary dyskinesia
Defective cilia (Kartagener) impair oocyte transport → subfertility & ectopic risk
Tubal ligation
Surgical division/occlusion of the tube for permanent contraception
Why ectopics cluster in the ampulla: the fertilised egg normally implants in the uterus after tubal transport — if scarring or ciliary failure delays transport, it implants in the ampulla instead.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Labyrinthine mucosal folds + ciliated & peg cells, NO glands = fallopian tube (richest folds in the ampulla).
Ciliated cells beat toward the uterus (transport); peg/secretory cells nourish & capacitate.
Oestrogen → ciliation; progesterone → secretion/deciliation.
Four regions: infundibulum (fimbriae) → ampulla → isthmus → intramural.
Ampulla = fertilisation site and commonest site of ectopic pregnancy.
Fimbriae on the infundibulum capture the ovulated oocyte.
Muscularis = inner circular + outer longitudinal; peristalsis + cilia move the oocyte.
STIC at the fimbrial end → high-grade serous carcinoma (p53); PID → scarring, ectopic, hydrosalpinx.
REPRODUCTIVE__Placenta:
Overview — The Fetomaternal Organ

The placenta is the interface for gas, nutrient and waste exchange, a major endocrine organ, and an immune barrier. It is built from two parts:

🔬 Image slot — placenta — branching chorionic villi (fetal) suspended in the intervillous space bathed by maternal blood over the decidua basalis
Fetal part
  • Chorion frondosum → the chorionic villi
  • Carries fetal blood in villous capillaries
Maternal part
  • Decidua basalis (decidualised endometrium)
  • Supplies maternal blood via spiral arteries
The human placenta is haemochorial: maternal blood directly bathes the trophoblast of the villi in the intervillous space — fetal and maternal blood never mix.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — chorionic villi — each covered by outer syncytiotrophoblast and inner cytotrophoblast, with a core of fetal capillaries and Hofbauer cells
  • Chorionic villi (tree-like profiles) floating in an intervillous space filled with maternal blood.
  • Each villus is covered by two trophoblast layers: outer syncytiotrophoblast + inner cytotrophoblast.
  • A villous core of fetal capillaries, mesenchyme and Hofbauer cells (fetal macrophages).
Chorionic villi suspended in a maternal-blood-filled intervillous space → placenta. Confirm the two trophoblast layers and the fetal capillaries in the core.
The Chorionic Villus & Its Trophoblast
Syncytiotrophoblast
Outer, multinucleated, no cell borders; contacts maternal blood; microvillous brush border; makes hormones & does transport
Cytotrophoblast (Langhans)
Inner mitotic stem cells that replenish the syncytiotrophoblast; prominent early, diminish with gestation
Villous core
Fetal capillaries + mesenchyme + Hofbauer cells (fetal macrophages)
Syncytiotrophoblast = the working surface (hormones + exchange, formed by fusion of cytotrophoblast); cytotrophoblast = the stem-cell reserve. As pregnancy advances the cytotrophoblast thins away, streamlining the barrier.
The Placental (Materno-Fetal) Barrier
🔬 Image slot — placental barrier — early thick barrier (syncytio + cyto + basement membrane + core + fetal endothelium) vs the thinned term barrier
Early (thick)
  • Syncytiotrophoblast → cytotrophoblast → basement membrane
  • → villous connective tissue → fetal capillary endothelium
Term (thin)
  • Thinned syncytiotrophoblast + fused basement membranes + fetal endothelium
  • Cytotrophoblast largely gone → efficient exchange
The barrier thins toward term (loss of cytotrophoblast, fusion of basement membranes) to maximise diffusion just as fetal demand peaks.
Circulation, Decidua & Spiral Arteries
🔬 Image slot — placental circulation — maternal spiral arteries opening into the intervillous space, and fetal blood in villous capillaries via the umbilical vessels
  • Maternal blood: spiral arteries → intervillous space (bathes the villi) → endometrial veins.
  • Fetal blood: two umbilical arteries (deoxygenated) → villous capillaries → one umbilical vein (oxygenated) back to the fetus.
  • Extravillous trophoblast invades and remodels the spiral arteries into wide, low-resistance channels for high flow.
Failure of spiral-artery remodelling leaves high-resistance vessels → placental under-perfusion → pre-eclampsia and fetal growth restriction (IUGR).
Placental Hormones & the Umbilical Cord
  • hCG — maintains the corpus luteum in early pregnancy (basis of pregnancy tests).
  • Human placental lactogen (hPL) — induces maternal insulin resistance (contributes to gestational diabetes) to spare glucose for the fetus.
  • Progesterone & oestrogen — maintain the pregnancy and prepare the breast; the placenta takes over from the corpus luteum by the second trimester.
  • Umbilical cord: two arteries + one vein embedded in Wharton’s jelly (mucoid connective tissue) that cushions the vessels.
All these hormones are made by the syncytiotrophoblast. A single umbilical artery is associated with congenital (esp. renal/cardiac) anomalies.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Pre-eclampsia
Inadequate spiral-artery remodelling → ischaemic placenta → hypertension, proteinuria, IUGR
Placenta accreta spectrum
Absent decidua → villi invade myometrium (accreta → increta → percreta); severe PPH risk
Placenta praevia / abruption
Low-lying placenta (praevia) or premature separation (abruption) → antepartum haemorrhage
Complete hydatidiform mole
All paternal (46,XX), no fetus; diffuse villous oedema (“bunch of grapes”) + trophoblast proliferation; ↑↑hCG; choriocarcinoma risk
Partial mole
Triploid; some fetal parts; focal villous swelling & milder trophoblast proliferation
Choriocarcinoma
Malignant trophoblast; ↑hCG; early haematogenous spread (lungs)
Chorioamnionitis / villitis
Infection of the membranes/villi (e.g. ascending bacteria, TORCH organisms)
Rhesus disease
Maternal anti-D crosses the placenta → fetal haemolysis (erythroblastosis fetalis / hydrops)
⭐ Exam Pearls
Chorionic villi in a maternal-blood intervillous space = placenta.
Villus = outer syncytiotrophoblast (hormones + exchange) + inner cytotrophoblast (stem cells) + core (fetal capillaries + Hofbauer cells).
Haemochorial: maternal blood directly contacts the syncytiotrophoblast; blood never mixes.
The barrier thins at term (cytotrophoblast disappears).
Extravillous trophoblast remodels spiral arteries; failure → pre-eclampsia / IUGR.
Hormones (syncytiotrophoblast): hCG (corpus luteum), hPL (insulin resistance / GDM), progesterone & oestrogen.
Cord = 2 arteries + 1 vein + Wharton’s jelly; single artery → anomaly association.
Complete mole = all paternal, no fetus, ↑↑hCG, choriocarcinoma risk; partial mole = triploid with fetal parts.
REPRODUCTIVE__Breast (resting & lactatin:
Overview — A Modified Sweat Gland

The breast is a modified apocrine sweat gland — a compound tubuloalveolar gland built to make milk. It is organised into 15–20 lobes, each draining by a lactiferous duct to the nipple, all set in a fibrofatty stroma.

🔬 Image slot — breast at low power — terminal duct lobular units (glands) scattered in an abundant fibrofatty stroma, ducts converging toward the nipple

Its functional unit is the terminal duct lobular unit (TDLU) — a terminal duct plus its cluster of acini — which is both the site of milk production and the origin of most breast disease.

The gland is hormone-responsive: it is quiet (stroma-rich) at rest and transforms into a crowded, secretory organ during pregnancy and lactation.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — TDLU — a terminal duct and its acini lined by two cell layers: inner luminal epithelial cells and outer myoepithelial cells, in loose intralobular stroma
  • Terminal duct lobular units (TDLUs) — clusters of small acini around a terminal duct — embedded in stroma.
  • Ducts and acini are lined by two cell layers: an inner luminal epithelial layer and an outer myoepithelial layer.
  • Abundant fibrofatty stroma (dense fibrous CT + adipose) in the resting gland.
Two-layered ducts/acini (luminal + myoepithelial) in a fibrofatty stroma → breast. The presence of an intact myoepithelial layer is also how pathologists tell in situ from invasive carcinoma.
The TDLU & Duct System
1
Acini + terminal ductule = TDLUthe hormone-responsive functional unit
2
Terminal → segmental ductsdraining each lobule/lobe
3
Lactiferous duct & sinuswiden behind the nipple, then open at it
Luminal epithelial cells
  • Inner secretory layer — make & secrete milk
Myoepithelial cells
  • Outer contractile layer on the basement membrane
  • Contract under oxytocin to eject milk
Most breast pathology (cysts, hyperplasia, carcinoma) arises in the TDLU. The lactiferous ducts near the nipple are lined by stratified squamous at their opening.
Resting vs Lactating Breast
🔬 Image slot — resting vs lactating breast — sparse small acini in dense stroma vs enlarged secretion-filled alveoli crowding out the stroma
Resting (inactive)
  • Stroma predominates (dense fibrous CT + fat)
  • Small, sparse acini; mostly ducts
  • Minor cyclical changes (luteal-phase oedema/proliferation)
Lactating (active)
  • Alveoli enlarge & fill with milk; vacuolated secretory epithelium
  • Stroma reduced — glands crowd it out
  • Colostrum (IgA-rich) precedes mature milk
Resting = stroma-rich with sparse small acini; lactating = expanded secretion-filled alveoli with scant stroma. The gland:stroma ratio flips with function.
Hormonal Control & Milk Secretion
  • Oestrogen → duct growth; progesterone → lobuloalveolar (acinar) development — both rise in pregnancy.
  • Prolactin → drives milk synthesis; high placental oestrogen/progesterone block milk secretion until delivery.
  • Oxytocin → myoepithelial contraction → milk ejection (“let-down”) — a neuroendocrine reflex triggered by suckling.
Merocrine (protein)
  • Casein & proteins by exocytosis (no cytoplasm lost)
Apocrine (lipid)
  • Milk fat released in an apical cap of cytoplasm
Prolactin makes the milk; oxytocin ejects it. Milk uses two secretion modes at once — merocrine for protein, apocrine for fat.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Fibroadenoma
Commonest benign tumour in young women; mobile “breast mouse”; proliferation of stroma + glands
Fibrocystic change
Commonest breast condition; cysts, apocrine metaplasia & fibrosis; lumpy, cyclical pain
Invasive ductal carcinoma
Commonest breast cancer; arises from the TDLU; loss of myoepithelium = invasion; desmoplasia
DCIS / lobular carcinoma
DCIS confined by an intact basement membrane; lobular types lose E-cadherin (single-file cells)
Intraductal papilloma
Benign duct lesion → bloody nipple discharge
Lactational mastitis / abscess
Staph. aureus via a cracked nipple during breastfeeding
Fat necrosis
After trauma/surgery; a firm lump that mimics cancer clinically
Paget’s disease of the nipple
Malignant (Paget) cells in the nipple epidermis — a sign of underlying ductal carcinoma
Breast cancer is classified by receptors — ER, PR and HER2 — which guide endocrine (tamoxifen/aromatase-inhibitor) and anti-HER2 (trastuzumab) therapy; triple-negative carries a worse prognosis.
⭐ Exam Pearls
The breast is a modified apocrine sweat gland (compound tubuloalveolar).
TDLU = functional unit AND origin of most breast pathology.
Two-cell lining: inner luminal epithelial (secretory) + outer myoepithelial (contractile).
Resting = stroma-rich, sparse small acini; lactating = expanded secretion-filled alveoli, scant stroma.
Oestrogen → ducts; progesterone → alveoli; prolactin → milk; oxytocin → ejection (myoepithelial).
Milk secretion: merocrine (protein) + apocrine (fat).
Invasive ductal carcinoma = commonest cancer; loss of myoepithelium marks invasion; classify by ER/PR/HER2.
Fibroadenoma = commonest benign tumour; fibrocystic change = commonest overall.
REPRODUCTIVE__Prostate Gland:
Overview — The Seminal-Fluid Gland

The prostate is the largest male accessory gland. It surrounds the prostatic urethra and secretes ~30% of the seminal fluid — a thin, milky, slightly acidic fluid rich in PSA, acid phosphatase, citrate and zinc.

🔬 Image slot — prostate at low power — tubuloalveolar glands with irregular lumina and corpora amylacea, set in an abundant fibromuscular stroma

It is a set of compound tubuloalveolar glands embedded in a prominent fibromuscular stroma (smooth muscle + fibrous tissue) that squeezes secretion into the urethra at ejaculation.

Two things name the prostate: two-cell glands with wavy lumina and corpora amylacea (lamellated concretions) sitting in those lumina.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — prostatic glands — two-cell epithelium (basal + luminal secretory), irregular infolded lumina, and a laminated corpus amylaceum
  • Glands/acini with irregular, infolded (“wavy”) lumina in a fibromuscular stroma.
  • A two-cell epithelium: a basal layer + a luminal (secretory) columnar layer.
  • Corpora amylacea — concentric, lamellated eosinophilic concretions in the lumina (increase with age; may calcify).
Two-cell glands with wavy lumina + corpora amylacea in a fibromuscular stroma → prostate. Whether the basal layer is present or lost is the crux of the benign-vs-malignant call.
The Two-Cell Glands & Corpora Amylacea
Luminal (secretory) cells
  • Tall columnar; secrete PSA, acid phosphatase & the seminal fluid
Basal cells
  • Flattened layer on the basement membrane (stem-cell reserve)
  • Lost in invasive adenocarcinoma
  • Corpora amylacea are lamellated glycoprotein concretions in the lumina — a normal, age-related finding (they can calcify into prostatic calculi).
Loss of the basal cell layer is the histological hallmark of invasive adenocarcinoma — benign glands keep their basal layer (confirmed by p63/high-molecular-weight cytokeratin stains).
The Zones (McNeal) & Secretions
🔬 Image slot — prostatic zones — peripheral (cancer), central, and transitional/periurethral (BPH) zones around the urethra
Peripheral zone (~70%)
Where most carcinomas arise; palpable on digital rectal examination
Central zone (~25%)
Surrounds the ejaculatory ducts
Transitional / periurethral (~5%)
Surrounds the urethra; the site of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)
  • PSA (prostate-specific antigen) is a serine protease that liquefies semen; it is the key serum tumour marker.
  • Other secretions: acid phosphatase, citrate, zinc and fibrinolysin.
Cancer = peripheral zone (palpable on DRE); BPH = transitional/periurethral zone (compresses the urethra). Their different locations explain why BPH obstructs early while cancer is often silent until advanced.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Benign prostatic hyperplasia
Transitional/periurethral nodular hyperplasia of glands + stroma (DHT-driven) → urinary hesitancy, frequency, nocturia
Prostatic adenocarcinoma
Peripheral zone; small crowded glands, loss of basal cells, prominent nucleoli, perineural invasion
Gleason grading
Grades tumour architecture (gland formation); the two commonest patterns are summed into the Gleason score
Metastasis
Osteoblastic (sclerotic) bone metastases; spread via the Batson vertebral venous plexus
Prostatitis
Acute/chronic inflammation; may raise PSA and cause pelvic pain
Corpora amylacea
Benign, age-related luminal concretions (not pathological)
PSA rises in cancer, BPH and prostatitis — it is organ-specific, not cancer-specific. BPH is treated with alpha-blockers and 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors (block DHT).
⭐ Exam Pearls
Two-cell glands (basal + luminal) with wavy lumina + corpora amylacea in a fibromuscular stroma = prostate.
Loss of the basal cell layer = invasive adenocarcinoma (basal markers p63/HMWCK negative).
Cancer = peripheral zone (palpable on DRE); BPH = transitional/periurethral zone (urethral obstruction).
BPH is DHT-driven → treated with 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors + alpha-blockers.
PSA = serine protease that liquefies semen; raised in cancer, BPH and prostatitis (organ- not cancer-specific).
Gleason grading scores tumour architecture; perineural invasion is characteristic.
Prostate cancer gives osteoblastic (sclerotic) bone metastases (via the Batson venous plexus).
Corpora amylacea are benign, age-related concretions — not a sign of disease.
REPRODUCTIVE__Cervix:
Overview — The Gateway Between Uterus & Vagina

The cervix is the lower neck of the uterus opening into the vagina. Its whole exam relevance turns on two different epithelia meeting — and the unstable junction between them.

🔬 Image slot — cervix — squamous ectocervix meeting the glandular endocervix at the squamocolumnar junction / transformation zone
Ectocervix
  • Faces the vagina; stratified squamous (non-keratinised)
Endocervix
  • Lines the canal; simple columnar mucus cells + glands
Where the two meet is the squamocolumnar junction / transformation zone — the site of metaplasia, HPV infection, dysplasia (CIN), cancer, and where the smear is taken.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — cervical epithelia — glycogen-rich stratified squamous ectocervix and mucus-secreting columnar endocervix with branching crypts, meeting at the SCJ
  • Ectocervix: non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium (glycogen-rich).
  • Endocervix: simple columnar mucus-secreting cells with deep branching endocervical glands (crypts).
  • An abrupt squamocolumnar junction where squamous meets columnar.
  • A fibromuscular stroma that is mostly fibrous (little smooth muscle, unlike the uterine body).
Squamous ectocervix + glandular endocervix meeting at a junction → cervix. The junctional (transformation) zone is the money spot for pathology.
Ectocervix vs Endocervix
Ectocervix (portio vaginalis)
Non-keratinised stratified squamous; glycogen-rich (stains brown with iodine — Schiller test); continuous with the vagina
Endocervix
Simple columnar mucus cells lining the canal + deep branching glands; mucus changes with the cycle
Cervical mucus is hormone-controlled: oestrogen (mid-cycle) makes it thin & watery (ferns, sperm-friendly); progesterone makes it thick & scanty (a barrier).
The Transformation Zone (High-Yield)
🔬 Image slot — transformation zone — original squamocolumnar junction, an ectropion of exposed columnar epithelium, and squamous metaplasia forming the new junction
  • Under oestrogen the columnar epithelium everts onto the ectocervix (ectropion/ectopy) and is exposed to the acidic vagina.
  • The exposed columnar cells undergo squamous metaplasia, forming the transformation zone between the old and new junctions.
  • These metaplastic cells are the target of HPV — so dysplasia (CIN) and cancer begin here.
The transformation zone is where HPV drives CIN → cervical cancer, and is exactly what the smear samples. Squamous metaplasia itself is normal/physiological.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Cervical ectropion
Columnar epithelium on the ectocervix (oestrogen, pregnancy, COCP) → friable, post-coital bleeding
Nabothian cysts
Mucus-retention cysts when metaplastic squamous epithelium blocks endocervical gland openings
CIN
Cervical intra-epithelial neoplasia (CIN 1–3): HPV-driven dysplasia at the TZ; koilocytes are the cytopathic clue
Squamous cell carcinoma
Commonest cervical cancer; arises from the TZ; driven by high-risk HPV
Adenocarcinoma
From endocervical glandular cells; also HPV-related; harder to detect on smear
Cervicitis
Inflammation, often Chlamydia/gonorrhoea; discharge & contact bleeding
HPV 16 & 18 drive most cervical cancer: viral E6 inactivates p53 and E7 inactivates Rb. Screening samples the TZ (smear/HPV test); the HPV vaccine targets 16/18 (and others).
⭐ Exam Pearls
Ectocervix = stratified squamous; endocervix = simple columnar + mucous glands.
Transformation zone (squamocolumnar junction) = metaplasia, HPV, CIN, cancer & smear-sampling site.
Squamous metaplasia of exposed columnar cells is normal; HPV then targets these cells.
Ectropion = columnar on the ectocervix (oestrogen/COCP/pregnancy) → contact bleeding.
Nabothian cysts = blocked endocervical glands (mucus retention).
HPV 16/18 → CIN → SCC; E6 inactivates p53, E7 inactivates Rb; koilocytes signal HPV.
Glycogen-rich squamous stains brown with iodine (Schiller test); abnormal areas do not.
Cervical mucus: oestrogen → thin/watery (ferns); progesterone → thick/scanty.
